The given statement is of the form \(a \to b\) with \(a \equiv \sim q\) and \(b \equiv p\).
The negation of \(a \to b\) is \(a \wedge \sim b\) (since \(a \to b \equiv \sim a \vee b\), so \(\sim(a \to b) \equiv a \wedge \sim b\)).
Therefore
\(\sim(\sim q \to p) \equiv \sim q \wedge \sim p\).
Final answer: \(\sim q \wedge \sim p\).

By De Morgan's law, \(\sim(a \wedge b) \equiv \sim a \vee \sim b\).
Here \(a \equiv p,\ b \equiv \sim q\), so
\(\sim(p \wedge \sim q) \equiv \sim p \vee \sim(\sim q) \equiv \sim p \vee q\) (using the law of double negation \(\sim(\sim q) \equiv q\)).
Final answer: \(\sim p \vee q\).

By De Morgan's law, \(\sim(a \vee b) \equiv \sim a \wedge \sim b\).
Here \(a \equiv p,\ b \equiv \sim q\), so
\(\sim(p \vee \sim q) \equiv \sim p \wedge \sim(\sim q) \equiv \sim p \wedge q\) (by double negation).
Final answer: \(\sim p \wedge q\).

By De Morgan's law, \(\sim(a \wedge b) \equiv \sim a \vee \sim b\).
With \(a \equiv p \vee \sim q\) and \(b \equiv r\):
\(\sim[(p \vee \sim q) \wedge r] \equiv \sim(p \vee \sim q) \vee \sim r\).
Applying De Morgan and double negation to \(\sim(p \vee \sim q) \equiv \sim p \wedge q\):
\(\equiv (\sim p \wedge q) \vee \sim r\).
Final answer: \((\sim p \wedge q) \vee \sim r\).

The statement has the form \(a \to b\) with \(a \equiv p\) and \(b \equiv p \vee \sim q\).
Negation of \(a \to b\) is \(a \wedge \sim b\):
\(\sim[p \to (p \vee \sim q)] \equiv p \wedge \sim(p \vee \sim q)\).
By De Morgan and double negation, \(\sim(p \vee \sim q) \equiv \sim p \wedge q\), so
\(\equiv p \wedge (\sim p \wedge q)\).
Final answer: \(p \wedge (\sim p \wedge q)\) (which is a contradiction, since \(p \wedge \sim p \equiv F\), consistent with the original being a tautology).

The statement is \(a \vee b\) with \(a \equiv \sim(p \wedge q)\) and \(b \equiv p \vee \sim q\).
By De Morgan, \(\sim(a \vee b) \equiv \sim a \wedge \sim b\):
\(\sim[\sim(p \wedge q) \vee (p \vee \sim q)] \equiv \sim(\sim(p \wedge q)) \wedge \sim(p \vee \sim q)\).
Using double negation \(\sim(\sim(p \wedge q)) \equiv p \wedge q\), and \(\sim(p \vee \sim q) \equiv \sim p \wedge q\) (De Morgan + double negation):
\(\equiv (p \wedge q) \wedge (\sim p \wedge q)\).
Final answer: \((p \wedge q) \wedge (\sim p \wedge q)\) (a contradiction, since it contains \(p \wedge \sim p\)).

The statement has the form \(a \to b\) with \(a \equiv p \vee \sim q\) and \(b \equiv p \wedge \sim q\).
Negation of \(a \to b\) is \(a \wedge \sim b\):
\(\sim[(p \vee \sim q) \to (p \wedge \sim q)] \equiv (p \vee \sim q) \wedge \sim(p \wedge \sim q)\).
By De Morgan and double negation, \(\sim(p \wedge \sim q) \equiv \sim p \vee q\), so
\(\equiv (p \vee \sim q) \wedge (\sim p \vee q)\).
Final answer: \((p \vee \sim q) \wedge (\sim p \vee q)\).

The statement is \(a \vee b\) with \(a \equiv \sim p \vee \sim q\) and \(b \equiv p \wedge \sim q\).
By De Morgan, \(\sim(a \vee b) \equiv \sim a \wedge \sim b\):
\(\sim[(\sim p \vee \sim q) \vee (p \wedge \sim q)] \equiv \sim(\sim p \vee \sim q) \wedge \sim(p \wedge \sim q)\).
Now \(\sim(\sim p \vee \sim q) \equiv p \wedge q\) and \(\sim(p \wedge \sim q) \equiv \sim p \vee q\) (De Morgan + double negation):
\(\equiv (p \wedge q) \wedge (\sim p \vee q)\).
Final answer: \((p \wedge q) \wedge (\sim p \vee q)\).

Let \(p\): a man is a judge, \(q\): he is honest. The statement is \(p \to q\).
Using \(p \to q \equiv \sim p \vee q\), we rewrite it without if...then:
\"A man is not a judge or he is honest.\"
Final answer: A man is not a judge or he is honest.

Let \(p\): 2 is a rational number, \(q\): \(\sqrt{2}\) is an irrational number. The statement is \(p \to q\).
Using \(p \to q \equiv \sim p \vee q\):
\"2 is not a rational number or \(\sqrt{2}\) is an irrational number.\"
Final answer: 2 is not a rational number or \(\sqrt{2}\) is an irrational number.

Let \(p\): \(f(2) = 0\), \(q\): \(f(x)\) is divisible by \((x - 2)\). The statement is \(p \to q\).
Using \(p \to q \equiv \sim p \vee q\):
\"\(f(2) \neq 0\) or \(f(x)\) is divisible by \((x - 2)\).\"
Final answer: \(f(2) \neq 0\) or \(f(x)\) is divisible by \((x - 2)\).

To prove: \(p \leftrightarrow q \equiv (p \wedge q) \vee (\sim p \wedge \sim q)\).
Start from \(p \leftrightarrow q \equiv (p \to q) \wedge (q \to p)\).
Using \(a \to b \equiv \sim a \vee b\):
\(\equiv (\sim p \vee q) \wedge (\sim q \vee p)\).
Expand by the distributive law:
\(\equiv [(\sim p \vee q) \wedge \sim q] \vee [(\sim p \vee q) \wedge p]\)
\(\equiv [(\sim p \wedge \sim q) \vee (q \wedge \sim q)] \vee [(\sim p \wedge p) \vee (q \wedge p)]\).
Since \(q \wedge \sim q \equiv F\) and \(\sim p \wedge p \equiv F\), and \(a \vee F \equiv a\):
\(\equiv (\sim p \wedge \sim q) \vee (q \wedge p)\)
\(\equiv (p \wedge q) \vee (\sim p \wedge \sim q)\) (commutativity).
Hence proved: \(p \leftrightarrow q \equiv (p \wedge q) \vee (\sim p \wedge \sim q)\).

To prove: \((p \vee q) \wedge (p \vee \sim q) \equiv p\).
By the distributive law \(a \vee (b \wedge c) \equiv (a \vee b) \wedge (a \vee c)\), taken in reverse:
\((p \vee q) \wedge (p \vee \sim q) \equiv p \vee (q \wedge \sim q)\).
Since \(q \wedge \sim q \equiv F\) (complement law):
\(\equiv p \vee F\).
By the identity law \(p \vee F \equiv p\):
\(\equiv p\).
Hence proved: \((p \vee q) \wedge (p \vee \sim q) \equiv p\).

To prove: \((p \wedge q) \vee (\sim p \wedge q) \vee (p \wedge \sim q) \equiv p \vee q\).
Group the first two terms and apply the distributive law:
\((p \wedge q) \vee (\sim p \wedge q) \equiv (p \vee \sim p) \wedge q \equiv T \wedge q \equiv q\) (complement law \(p \vee \sim p \equiv T\) and identity law).
So the expression becomes \(q \vee (p \wedge \sim q)\).
By the distributive law \(a \vee (b \wedge c) \equiv (a \vee b) \wedge (a \vee c)\):
\(q \vee (p \wedge \sim q) \equiv (q \vee p) \wedge (q \vee \sim q) \equiv (q \vee p) \wedge T \equiv q \vee p\).
Hence \(\equiv p \vee q\) (commutativity).
Hence proved: \((p \wedge q) \vee (\sim p \wedge q) \vee (p \wedge \sim q) \equiv p \vee q\).

To prove: \(\sim[(p \vee \sim q) \to (p \wedge \sim q)] \equiv (p \vee \sim q) \wedge (\sim p \vee q)\).
The left side is the negation of \(a \to b\) with \(a \equiv p \vee \sim q,\ b \equiv p \wedge \sim q\).
Negation of \(a \to b\) is \(a \wedge \sim b\):
\(\sim[(p \vee \sim q) \to (p \wedge \sim q)] \equiv (p \vee \sim q) \wedge \sim(p \wedge \sim q)\).
By De Morgan's law and double negation, \(\sim(p \wedge \sim q) \equiv \sim p \vee q\).
Therefore
\(\equiv (p \vee \sim q) \wedge (\sim p \vee q)\).
Hence proved: \(\sim[(p \vee \sim q) \to (p \wedge \sim q)] \equiv (p \vee \sim q) \wedge (\sim p \vee q)\).
